Stochastic process ((Xt​)t∈T​)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Probability theory
OurBigBook.com Words: 41k Articles: 730
A stochastic process describes uncertainty about a whole history: not just the probability distribution of a measurement now, but how measurements at different times fit together. It is a family (Xt​)t∈T​ of random variables on one probability space, with index set T. Time is the usual index: T={0,1,2,…} for successive observations or T=[0,∞) for continuous time. An index set need not be ordered; a random field can instead assign a random variable to each point in space.
There are two complementary views. Fix a time t and Xt​ is a random variable; fix a sample space outcome ω and t↦Xt​(ω) is one sample path. A model specifies the probability distribution of these histories. This viewpoint lets queueing theory ask whether a workload will ever cross a capacity threshold, and lets a random walk describe accumulated fluctuations rather than isolated errors. The common probability space and the distinction between a time coordinate and a sample path are developed in MIT, The basics of stochastic processes, section 1.
A concrete construction starts with a Bernoulli process of independent fair bits B1​,B2​,…. Keeping Bn​ records the next trial; adding the signs gives a simple random walk on the integer line, S0​=0 and Sn​=∑j=1n​(2Bj​−1). Every increment of this random walk is ±1, yet the positions are dependent: Sn+1​ contains all the previous increments. Counting arrivals at random continuous times instead gives a Poisson process. These examples separate three questions: what values are possible, how time is indexed, and how the values depend on one another.
For the fair simple random walk on the integer line, the expected value is ESn​=0 and the variance is Var(Sn​)=n. At time four, returning to zero requires exactly two positive steps, so P(S4​=0)=(24​)/24=3/8. A rate-two Poisson process instead has P(N1​=0)=e−2≈0.1353. A single realized sample path does not establish either probability: they follow from the specified joint probability distributions.
The most revealing feature is often dependence. Two stochastic processes can have identical marginal distributions at every time while one forgets everything at the next step and the other repeats its first value forever. Their finite-dimensional distributions and covariance functions distinguish them. That extra structure is what makes a stochastic process useful for prediction.

Pólya urn model (Xn​=Bn​/(Bn​+Rn​),E[Xn+1​∣Fn​]=Xn​)

Words: 183 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
Begin with positive counts of two colours. At each step select one ball uniformly and replace it together with one new ball of its colour. If the total initial count is m, the blue proportion satisfies Xn+1​−Xn​=(In+1​−Xn​)/(m+n+1), where the next blue indicator has conditional mean Xn​. Thus Xn​ is a bounded martingale and converges almost surely and in L2 to a random proportion. If uniforms generate the draws, the update from time n to n+1 must use the fresh Un+1​ relative to Fn​=σ(U1​,…,Un​).

Positivity of the limiting Pólya urn proportion (B0​,R0​>0⟹P(0<X∞​<1)=1)

Words: 96
Pólya urn model OurBigBook.com
Both colour counts tend to infinity almost surely. For example, Xn​≥B0​/(m+n), and independent events Un+1​≤B0​/[2(n+1)] occur infinitely often by the Borel-Cantelli second lemma, forcing infinitely many blue additions.
The martingale increment formula gives E[(Xk+1​−Xk​)2∣Fk​]≤Xk​/(m+k+1)2. Conditional orthogonality of later increments and E[Xk​∣Fn​]=Xn​ imply
E[(X∞​−Xn​)2∣Fn​]≤Xn​∑j=m+n+1∞​j−2≤m+nXn​​.
(1)
On X∞​=0 the squared difference is Xn2​, so its conditional probability is at most 1/[(m+n)Xn​]=1/Bn​→0. Dominated convergence proves zero probability of that endpoint. The symmetric argument for red excludes X∞​=1. No explicit beta law is needed for this proof.

Chaining (Xt​−Xt0​​=∑k​(Xπk​(t)​−Xπk−1​(t)​))

Words: 85
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A multiscale method for bounding the supremum of a stochastic process. Approximate each index by points πk​(t) in successively finer metric nets, expand its difference from an anchor as a telescoping sum, and bound the largest increment at each scale. For a finite index set the finest net can be the entire set, making this decomposition exact. If Ek​ is the set of approximation edges, then pointwise supt​(Xt​−Xt0​​)≤∑k​max(u,v)∈Ek​​(Xu​−Xv​). Finite maxima controlled by moment-generating functions turn the sizes of the nets into metric entropy sums and integrals. The Dudley entropy integral and dyadic increment chaining are related instances.

Random sequential adsorption

Stochastic process OurBigBook.com

Mean reversion

Words: 69
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
Mean reversion is a tendency for a stochastic process to move back towards a reference level. For an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, the conditional expected value of a future deviation is the present deviation multiplied by e−θh after time h. Individual sample paths can move away from that level: mean reversion describes a conditional tendency, not monotone motion or a guaranteed return by a deadline. It also does not by itself imply a stationary process; the initial probability distribution matters.

Bernoulli process (Bn​∼iidBernoulli(p))

Words: 78
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A Bernoulli process is a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with a Bernoulli distribution: P(Bn​=1)=p and P(Bn​=0)=1−p. It models repeated Bernoulli trials with a fixed success probability and no dependence between trials. The count Kn​=∑j=1n​Bj​ has a binomial distribution, expected value np, and variance np(1−p); the first success time has a geometric distribution on {1,2,…}. The observations Bn​ and the accumulated count Kn​ are different stochastic processes: the observations are independent, while consecutive counts share all earlier observations. [ref]

Skorokhod problem

Words: 116 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
Find a constrained path and a boundary regulator which together modify a given driving path. In the half-line case, write x=g+k≥0, require k(0)=0 and k nondecreasing, and require its increases to occur only where x=0. For multidimensional orthants the regulator acts through a specified reflection matrix. The Skorokhod reflection map on the half-line solves the one-dimensional continuous-path case explicitly.

Skorokhod reflection map on the half-line (Γ(g)(t)=g(t)+sups≤t​[−g(s)]+)

Words: 61
Skorokhod problem OurBigBook.com
For a continuous driving path with g(0)≥0, the running supremum supplies the minimal nondecreasing regulator keeping the path nonnegative. It increases only at a new negative running minimum, where the reflected path is zero. Any regulator satisfying the Skorokhod problem constraints must coincide with it. On a finite time interval, ∥Γ(g)−Γ(h)∥∞​≤2∥g−h∥∞​, so the map is continuous and transfers a functional central limit theorem to reflected workloads.

Self-similarity of a stochastic process (Z(a⋅)=daHZ)

Words: 67
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A process Z is self-similar with exponent H if Z(a⋅) and aHZ have the same finite-dimensional distributions for every a>0, or the same path law when the process is considered as a random path. Fractional Brownian motion has this property with its Hurst exponent. It converts dilation of time to deterministic scaling of amplitude: Z(N⋅)/N=dNH−1Z. Consequently a small-noise large deviation principle with inverse-variance speed produces the large-deviation speed N2(1−H) for those rescaled paths.

Random field

Words: 42
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A random field is a family of random variables indexed by points of a spatial domain, or more generally by a multi-dimensional parameter set. Its componentwise covariance function and spectral tensor describe second-order dependence. A Gaussian random field has jointly Gaussian finite-dimensional distributions; a general random field need not be Gaussian.

Locally bounded process

Words: 47
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A process is locally bounded if there are stopping times τn​↑∞ and finite deterministic constants Kn​ bounding it on the stopped intervals. A locally bounded predictable process is integrable against a semimartingale. Continuous adapted processes are locally bounded by stopping their magnitudes and time.

Branching process

Words: 289 Articles: 4
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A stochastic process in which individuals independently produce offspring according to specified distributions. It models growing populations and gives an approximation to sparse percolation clusters when collisions between branches can be neglected. On a lattice, loops and overlapping branches prevent this approximation from being an exact identity.

Critical branching process (m=1)

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Branching process OurBigBook.com
A branching process with mean offspring number one. In a continuous-time birth–death example with equal per-cell birth and death rates β, one initial individual has survival probability 1/(1+βt) and mean size 1+βt conditional on survival.

Distribution of a critical linear birth-death population (P0​=1+λtλt​,Pn​=(1+λt)n+1(λt)n−1​ (n≥1))

Words: 58
Critical branching process OurBigBook.com
For equal individual birth and death rates λ and one initial individual, the probability generating function is F(z,t)=1−(1−z)/[1+λt(1−z)]. It solves Ft​=λ(z−1)2Fz​ with F(z,0)=z, and its geometric expansion gives the displayed probabilities. The mean remains one and the variance is 2λt, although extinction occurs with probability tending to one. The surviving fraction 1/(1+λt) has conditional mean population 1+λt.

Multitype Poisson branching process (Bi​(Λ))

Words: 150 Articles: 1
Branching process OurBigBook.com
A particle of type i has independently a Poisson distribution of type-j offspring with mean λij​. Different particles reproduce independently. If pi(t)​ is the probability generation t is nonempty from one type-i ancestor, then p(0)=1 and p(t+1)=T(p(t)), where Ti​(x)=1−exp[−(Λx)i​]. This iteration decreases to the survival probability of a branching process, the greatest nonnegative fixed point of T. The expected type-count row vector in generation t is eiT​Λt.

Spectral survival criterion for multitype Poisson branching (∑i​pi​>0⟺ρ(Λ)>1)

Words: 87
Multitype Poisson branching process OurBigBook.com
This criterion holds even for reducible nonnegative matrices. If a fixed point p=0 exists, 1−e−z<z for z>0 gives (Λp)i​>pi​ on its support. Some α>1 therefore satisfies Λp≥αp, forcing the spectral radius above one by the Perron–Frobenius theorem. Conversely take v≥0, v=0, with Λv=ρv and ρ>1. For sufficiently small η>0, 1−e−ηρvi​≥ηvi​. Thus ηv is a subsolution; monotone iteration under T gives a positive fixed point below 1. Strictness of 1−e−z<z excludes survival at the critical value for this Poisson offspring law.

Unnormalized time autocorrelation (C(t,τ)=⟨X(t)X(t+τ)⟩)

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
The raw same-observable time correlation C(t,τ)=⟨X(t)X(t+τ)⟩. For a stationary process, it equals ⟨X⟩2+Cov(X(t),X(t+τ)). Its connected part is the autocovariance; unlike the normalized statistical autocorrelation, no division by the variance is imposed. The distinction matters for fluctuations around a nonzero equilibrium point.

Intrawell phase autocorrelation (C(τ)≃α2+(Teff​/κ)e−κ∣τ∣)

Words: 60
Unnormalized time autocorrelation OurBigBook.com
Near the stable Adler phase equation point α=arcsin(ω/ϵ), linearized noise obeys an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with relaxation rate κ=ϵ2−ω2​. Its harmonic-model raw correlation is α2+(Teff​/κ)e−κ∣τ∣. Nonlinear drift also shifts the local mean at order Tmeff​. This describes times after relaxation but before appreciable phase slips; it is not a stationary infinite-time correlation of the unwrapped phase at fixed nonzero noise.

Sample path (t↦Xt​(ω))

Words: 153
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
For a stochastic process Xt​ and a fixed sample space outcome ω, its sample path is the function t↦Xt​(ω). One row of observed fair bits, one trajectory of a random walk, or one staircase of Poisson process arrival counts is a sample path. Fixing t instead gives a random variable ranging across possible histories. The same two-variable object Xt​(ω) therefore describes both observations across outcomes and evolution within an outcome.
Statements about continuous, càdlàg or Hölder continuous function sample paths concern these functions simultaneously in time. They differ from assertions made at each fixed time separately. For example, take U with a uniform distribution on [0,1] and set Xt​=1{t=U}​. For every fixed t, Xt​=0 almost surely, but every sample path has a single spike. Thus this process is a modification of a stochastic process that is identically zero, while the two are not indistinguishable stochastic processes. Continuity of both sets of sample paths rules out this discrepancy: equality at a countable dense set then implies equality everywhere. This is why path regularity is an additional part of constructing a continuous-time model.

Bounded increments (∣Xn+1​−Xn​∣≤C(n≥0))

Words: 238 Articles: 2
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A discrete-time stochastic process has bounded increments if a single deterministic C<∞ satisfies ∣Xn+1​−Xn​∣≤C almost surely for every n. The constant is uniform in time and sample outcome; bounding each increment by a different constant does not suffice. This property applies to differences, so it does not require the process itself to stay bounded.

Bounded-increment martingale convergence-or-oscillation dichotomy (Xn​→X∞​∈RorliminfXn​=−∞, limsupXn​=+∞)

Words: 186 Articles: 1
Bounded increments OurBigBook.com
A discrete-time martingale with a common deterministic bound on all increments either converges finitely or has liminfXn​=−∞ and limsupXn​=+∞, almost surely. Stopping on first crossing below −A gives a lower bound −A−M on the overshoot. Adding A+M+X0−​ produces a nonnegative martingale, so the martingale convergence theorem forces finite convergence on the event of never crossing. Apply the same argument to −X.

Oscillation of a bounded centered iid random walk (liminfSn​=−∞,limsupSn​=+∞)

Words: 126
Bounded-increment martingale convergence-or-oscillation dichotomy OurBigBook.com
Let Sn​=∑j=1n​Xj​, where the increments are nonconstant independent and identically distributed random variables with zero expected value and ∣Xj​∣≤c. Then the random walk oscillates between arbitrarily large positive and negative levels almost surely. For Ta​=inf{n:Sn​≥a}, the stopped martingale a+c−Sn∧Ta​​ is nonnegative. The martingale convergence theorem implies that Sn​ converges finitely on {Ta​=∞}. However, some δ>0 has P(∣X1​∣>δ)>0, and the Borel-Cantelli lemmas imply ∣Xn​∣>δ infinitely often. Hence finite convergence is impossible. Apply this to every positive integer a and to −Sn​.
The bounded increments also imply infinitely many visits to [−c/2,c/2]: a path cannot cross from above c/2 to below −c/2 without entering this interval. Identical distribution cannot simply be dropped. For independent symmetric signs εj​, the increments Xj​=c4−(j−1)εj​ satisfy ∣Sn​∣≥2c/3 for every n, even though they are nonzero, independent, symmetric and uniformly bounded.

A random walk accumulates its one-step increments; a Poisson process has nonnegative integer increments counting arrivals in (s,t]. A process can have independent increments even though its values at different times are dependent.

Stationary increments

Words: 66
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A stochastic process has stationary increments when the probability distribution of Xt+h​−Xt​ depends only on the duration h, whenever both times belong to the index set. The clock origin then does not change the increment law. For Brownian motion, that law is N(0,h); for a rate-λ Poisson process, it is a Poisson distribution with expected value λh. Neither process itself is a stationary process: their variances grow with t. Stationary increments and a stationary process describe different properties.

Independent increments

Words: 76
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
A stochastic process has independent increments when, for every t0​<t1​<⋯<tk​, the random variables Xt1​​−Xt0​​,…,Xtk​​−Xtk−1​​ are independent. Adjacent intervals are allowed: each increment represents the change after its left endpoint up to its right endpoint. A Poisson process, Brownian motion, and a random walk with independent steps have this property. Their values at different times need not be independent: for a fair simple random walk on the integer line, Cov(Sm​,Sn​)=min(m,n) because both positions contain the same first min(m,n) increments. Independent increments need not be stationary increments; summing independent steps with time-dependent variances gives a counterexample.

Words: 255 Articles: 1
Stochastic process OurBigBook.com
For times t1​,…,tn​, the corresponding finite-dimensional distribution of a stochastic process X is the joint probability distribution of the random vector (Xt1​​,…,Xtn​​). The collection of these distributions records every finite set of coordinates of the process.
Knowing only the one-time marginal distributions is insufficient. Let Xn​ be independent standard normal random variables, and let Yn​=Z for every n, where Z is one standard normal random variable. Every Xn​ and Yn​ has the same standard normal distribution. Nevertheless, for m=n, the difference Xn​−Xm​ has a normal distribution with variance two, whereas Yn​−Ym​=0. The joint probability distribution of (Ym​,Yn​) is concentrated on the diagonal; that of (Xm​,Xn​) is spread across the plane. A model for tomorrow's value therefore needs the relation between observations as well as their separate distributions.
For a real-valued stochastic process, its finite-dimensional distributions determine its probability law on the product sigma-algebra. With an uncountable index set, a path property such as continuity need not be measurable in that sigma-algebra; specifying a suitable space of sample paths and a regular modification of a stochastic process is a separate step. This distinction is explained in MIT, The basics of stochastic processes, section 1.1.

Consistency means that discarding coordinates by marginalization agrees with the law already assigned to the smaller collection, and relabeling coordinates relabels the law. The theorem turns finite recipes into a complete stochastic process. In particular, products of one fixed probability distribution construct an independent and identically distributed sequence; putting one common random variable in every coordinate constructs the perfectly shared process above. The theorem supplies a law on the coordinate space, but does not by itself ensure continuous sample paths.

On (0,1]d, the dyadic filtration is generated by the partitions into half-open cubes of side 2−n. The conditional expectation of an integrable function is its average on each atom. Step functions on these partitions are dense in L1; approximation and the Doob maximal inequality show that their conditional averages converge in L1 and almost everywhere to the original function.

To extend it to the trivial time-zero sigma-algebra one must set X0​=1: applying the same displayed formula at zero instead gives 1(0,1/2]​, which is not adapted and has the wrong expected value. A stochastic process X is adapted to a filtration (Ft​) when Xt​ is Ft​-measurable at every time t. Its present value therefore depends only on information already available.

For an adapted process with right-continuous paths and a stopping time T, XtT​=Xt∧T​ is adapted. At fixed t, round t∧T upward on finite partitions of [0,t]. Every approximating value is Ft​-measurable, and right continuity gives the limit. Completeness handles a null exceptional set if right continuity holds only almost surely. A process H is progressively measurable when, for every T, its restriction to [0,T]×Ω is measurable for B([0,T])⊗FT​. Assign the stochastic process the path 1A​(t) at the null sample point and the zero path at the other point. Each fixed-time variable is measurable and the paths are càdlàg almost surely, but the stochastic process is not progressively measurable: a section in the time variable of a product-measurable function must be Borel measurable at every sample point. The zero stochastic process is an indistinguishable progressively measurable version. Completing the filtration does not complete the time-product sigma-algebra or remove this distinction.

Every approximation is jointly measurable for the terminal product sigma-algebra because all sampled values are FT​-measurable. Sampling from the right need not preserve adaptedness at intermediate times, but that is not required in this proof.

A real Lévy process with continuous paths is Brownian motion with deterministic linear drift: Xt​=bt+σWt​. Continuity forces the jump measure in the Lévy–Khintchine formula to vanish, leaving characteristic function exp(t(ibu−σ2u2/2)). If its law is also invariant under Xt​↦λ−1Xλ2t​ for every λ>0, then b=0. The zero-variance case is included.

Its Lévy measure is ∑j​λj​δzj​​, its mean is t(γ+∑j​λj​zj​), and its variance is t∑j​λj​zj2​. Its paths have finitely many jumps on every bounded interval and deterministic slope γ between jumps. Coincident mark sizes combine their rates; zero marks have no effect. The drift here uses the uncompensated finite-sum convention, which differs from the drift parameter in a compensated Lévy–Khintchine formula.

Finite increment vectors inherit their independent laws by convergence in distribution; the near-zero estimate supplies continuity at zero. Hence X has a càdlàg modification that is a Lévy process. A subordinator is a Lévy process with nondecreasing paths. Its nonnegative stationary increments have a Laplace transform of the form

where Φ is called its Laplace exponent. Its standard path convention is càdlàg. Subordinators provide random clocks for subordination of a Lévy process.

The Strong Markov property gives independent increments and stationary increments; the strict inverse of the continuous running maximum has càdlàg paths. The Brownian first-passage Laplace transform gives Laplace exponent Φ(λ)=2λ​, so the process is strictly stable of index 1/2. Choosing the non-strict hitting times preserves each fixed-level law but generally loses right continuity at random levels, as in the fixed-level versus simultaneous Brownian passage-time equality.
Countable dense jumps of the Brownian first-passage subordinator
Words: 129

The Brownian first-passage subordinator has a countable dense set of jump levels almost surely, and is continuous at every other level. Its paths are finite nondecreasing functions, so on a bounded level interval there can be only finitely many jumps larger than any fixed positive size; a countable union proves countability. For density, suppose its path were continuous throughout an open level interval. It is strictly increasing, since the original continuous Brownian path takes different values at different passage times. Its continuous inverse on that interval would parametrize a positive-length time interval on which the Brownian path increases monotonically. This contradicts nowhere monotonicity of Brownian motion. Thus every level interval contains a jump. In particular dense discontinuities do not mean that the path is nowhere continuous: it is continuous at every level outside a countable random set.
